notes: \cpara{Promises a simple trick that makes an unanswerable question solvable.}

\cpara{The trick: ask why you believe X instead of why X is so. The second question is ``guaranteed to have a real answer,'' even if X is false or incoherent. A similar method is old. Hume, for a philosophical term suspected of having no meaning: ``we need but enquire, from what impression is that supposed idea derived? And if it be impossible to assign any, this will serve to confirm our suspicion'' (\textsc{Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding}, 1748, section 2).}

\cpara{Explains why the second question is answerable: the belief exists, and some chain of causes leads to it. For free will, a book-length cognitive account of how the feeling of willing arises already existed (Daniel Wegner, 2002; see the note on ``Dissolving the Question'').}
\cpara{Offers four more pairs of questions: time, being born as oneself, consciousness, the existence of reality.}

\clogic{This pair is close to what David Chalmers later named ``the meta-problem of consciousness'': ``the problem of explaining why we think that there is a problem of consciousness'' (\textsc{Journal of Consciousness Studies}, 2018). Chalmers finds versions of the strategy in Hobbes, Hume, Spinoza and Kant. Whether answering the second question settles the first is the disputed point. Illusionists typically hold that it does; Chalmers holds that ``explaining our judgments about consciousness does not suffice to solve or dissolve the problem of consciousness.''}
\cpara{Says the method works whether or not the question is confused, and traces the author's belief about socks back through vision to the socks and why they were put on.}
\cpara{Concludes that the belief about socks is fully explained by the socks, as it should be, since information requires interaction.}
\cpara{The contrasting case: a mirage of a lake is explained without any lake, so the belief is ``explained away.''}
\cpara{Draws the common point: either way the belief is a real event with a causal history.}
\cpara{Restates the point with the lake: the question about the lake may fail, the question about the perception cannot.}
\cpara{Raises the objection: ``I believe in free will because I have free will.'' That, the post says, is not so easy.}
\cpara{Begins the answer: the perception of socks is an event in the visual cortex, open to cognitive science.}
\cpara{Continues: each step in the sock chain is explained by ordinary science, from biology and optics to thermodynamics.}
\cpara{States the requirement: break the causal chain into small steps, each explained in terms that are ``not themselves confusing,'' the standard of ``Dissolving the Question.''}
\cpara{Applies the requirement to free will: the sock detector is clear, so where is the free-will sensor, and how does it work? The questions are left to the reader.}
\cpara{Says that if the belief comes from observing something real, tracing back will ``eventually'' reach it.}
\cpara{Otherwise the tracing finds an algorithm that runs skew to reality.}
\cpara{Repeats that the question about the belief always has an answer, with the belief as the starting point.}
\cpara{Contrasts cognitive science, whose questions are ``solvable,'' with metaphysics.}
\cpara{Adds that the idea that cognitive science is less lofty than metaphysics ``is simply wrong.'' No reason is given.}
